html:
Genetic studies of old blood samples suggest that HIV, the virus that causes AIDS, crossed from central Africa to Haiti around 1966, and from there reached the United States around 1969, more than a decade before anyone knew the disease existed.

The pandemic strain of HIV began as a virus of chimpanzees in southeastern Cameroon. It passed to people, probably through hunting, early in the twentieth century, and spread quietly in Kinshasa, then called Léopoldville, in the Belgian Congo, helped by railways, river boats and a growing city.

After the Congo's independence in 1960, thousands of Haitian teachers and professionals went to work there, many leaving Haiti under the dictatorship of François Duvalier. Researchers think one infected person carried the virus home. It then spread in Haiti and on to the US, perhaps through travel or the blood plasma trade.

When the epidemic was recognised in 1981, Haitians were wrongly blamed as a risk group in themselves, a stigma that harmed Haiti's people and its tourist trade. See the AIDS epidemic.
